title: 2.5 EMISSIONS MARKETS
summary: Emissions markets emerged from international efforts, starting around 1990, to address global warming's threat to agriculture through a cap-and-trade structure resembling the historical commons problem, formalized by the Kyoto Protocol. The chapter traces how this structure forces contentious choices — how allocation disputes split along national and economic lines, why the cost of compliance has politically deadlocked broader climate agreement, and how governments intervene to steer prices — while noting that coal-fired generation is the market's real economic target, a fact underscored by how cheap fracked natural gas did more to displace coal than legislation did. It also covers the mechanics participants navigate: obtaining credits via allocation or offsets, reducing exposure through carbon capture (mechanical or biological), and managing the market's distinctive, limited role for speculation, including the risk of cornering and hedges against it. Finally, it places CO2 trading within a wider family of pollutant markets covering other greenhouse gases and pollutants like SOX and NOX.
provenance: rewritten orientation from this chapter's concept set; no new claims
